audits.claim: Section 1, Hawaiian row: the four Hawaiian sibling terms are kaikua'ana (elder) / kaikaina (younger, same sex) / kaikuahine (man's sister) / kaiku'a-ne (woman's brother), per Pukui & Elbert 1986.

audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (HTML; UH Hilo Wehewehe Wikiwiki headword list, 8 hits; companion negative query ?q=kaiku%CA%BB%C4%81ne retrieved, 0 hits)

audits.source_excerpt: n., Brother or male cousin of a female. ... 2. Brother or male cousin of a female (PE). 3. The brother of a sister (AP).
audits.basis: The row's substance holds for three terms: kaikua'ana 'Older sibling or cousin of the same sex', kaikaina 'Younger sibling or cousin of the same sex', kaikuahine 'Sister or female cousin of a male (PE)' all retrieve as glossed. The written form 'kaiku'a-ne' does not exist as a headword in the same dictionary, which returns no entry for it; the woman's-brother term is kaikuna-ne. Erratum appended to the entry 2026-10-17; original bytes preserved.
audits.access_limit: Pukui & Elbert (1986) data as published through the UH Hilo dictionary site; the 1986 print volume was not inspected, so no print pagination is cited.

audits.claim: Section 2, Hawaiian row: pi'o sibling marriage functions as rank-making ('Hawaiian pi'o sibling marriage as rank-making').

audits.source_excerpt: 2. n., Marriage of full brother and sister of nīʻaupiʻo rank, presumably the highest possible rank. Their offspring had the rank of naha, which is less than piʻo but probably more than nīʻaupiʻo.
audits.basis: Supports both halves of the entry's coupling of lexicon to rank ideology: pi'o names a full-brother/full-sister marriage, and the term is entangled with a rank ladder (ni-'aupi'o parents, naha offspring). audits.claim: Section 8 item 1: Sinitic kinship vocabulary sits in the written/law register (Japanese fubo, ryo-shin) while native terms carry plain speech (chichi/haha).
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (ja.wiktionary entry text; en.wiktionary headword 両親 retrieved separately for ryo-shin)
audits.source_locator: ja.wiktionary, headword 父母, Japanese section: reading and gloss line
audits.source_excerpt: 父母 (ふぼ) (家族) 父（ちち）と母（はは）。両親。 英語: parents
audits.basis: The Sinitic-character form is read fubo and glossed through the native morphemes chichi/haha plus ryo-shin, exactly the two-register split the entry describes. The separately retrieved en.wiktionary headword 両親 gives '両(りょう)親(しん) (ryo-shin) ... both parents' and marks 親 (oya) '(informal)', matching the entry's ryo-shin gloss.
audits.access_limit: Wiktionary is crowd-edited (cites NHK accent dictionary 1998, Kanjipedia 2015-). Shibatani 1990 was not retrieved, so the historical Confucian-law transmission story is not evidenced by this row, only the register split.

audits.claim: Section 8 item 1: the Korean borrowed stratum bu-mo coexists with native kin terms kept for the home register.
audits.source_locator: en.wiktionary, headword 부모, Korean section, Etymology sentence and Noun synonyms list
audits.source_excerpt: Sino-Korean word from 父母, largely displacing native 어버이 (eobeoi). ... Synonyms: 부모님 (bumonim, honorific), 어버이 (eobeoi, native equivalent)
audits.basis: Confirms a Sino-Korean term for 'parents' set against an explicit 'native equivalent', i.e. the borrowed/native register contrast the item asserts, and adds the honorific variant bu-mo-nim. The retrieval does not evidence the entry's specific native pair appa/eomma, which is a different lexeme set (아빠/엄마) than the one this page names.
audits.access_limit: Wiktionary (crowd-edited); Lee & Ramsey 2000 not retrieved; the appa/eomma pair named by the entry remains unrechecked.

audits.claim: Section 1, Sudanese row: Latin distinguishes patruus (FB) / avunculus (MB) / amita (FZ) / matertera (MZ), the descriptive fingerprint.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (en.wiktionary headword patruus; companion headword avunculus retrieved)
audits.source_locator: en.wiktionary, headwords patruus and avunculus, Latin section, noun sense 1 and coordinate-terms line
audits.source_excerpt: paternal uncle; a father's brother ... Coordinate terms: amita, avunculus, mātertera
audits.basis: patruus is FB; the companion retrieval gives avunculus '(Classical Latin) maternal uncle, mother's brother' and a coordinate line naming amita ('paternal aunt') and matertera ('maternal aunt'). That is the exact four-way FB/MB/FZ/MZ split the entry attributes to Latin, so the row's example supports the descriptive (Sudanese) label rather than merely a bibliography fact.
audits.access_limit: Wiktionary entries, though their references list Lewis & Short (1879) and Gaffiot (1934); Perseus, which hosts Lewis & Short, returned HTTP 503 on two attempts, so the classical dictionary itself was not read here.

audits.claim: Section 5: levirate = widow marries the deceased husband's brother, cited to Deuteronomy 25:5-10 and Genesis 38.
audits.retrieval_status: retrieved (Wikisource King James Version, book page; chapter 25 verses 5-10 read; Genesis 38:8 read from the companion Genesis page)
audits.source_locator: Wikisource 'Bible (King James)/Deuteronomy', chapter 25, verse 5 (vv.6-10 give the offspring rule and the refusal ritual); Genesis 38:8 on the Genesis page
audits.source_excerpt: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her
audits.basis: Verse 6 supplies the purpose (firstborn succeeds in the dead brother's name), vv.7-10 the refusal ritual, and Genesis 38:8 reads 'And Judah said unto Onan, Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.' Both citations are placed correctly and the institution is era/law coupling: a marriage rule that presupposes affinal categories.
audits.access_limit: Scripture text only (public-domain KJV via Wikisource); no historical-critical study of Israelite levirate practice was retrieved, and the entry's inferential point about building the affinal vocabulary first is not tested by this row.
